title: Kenyan Sorghum Ugali
community: Popular in Western Kenya, Eastern Kenya, and among pastoral communities
author: Mama Wanjiru
desc: Kenyan Sorghum Ugali — made from ground sorghum (mtama) flour, with a distinctive reddish-brown colour, slightly smoky flavour, and excellent nutritional profile. A traditional staple in parts of Western and Eastern Kenya.
longDesc: Sorghum ugali (ugali wa mtama) is darker and more intensely flavoured than white maize ugali, with a slight smokiness that many who grew up eating it consider deeply comforting. Sorghum has been cultivated in Kenya for thousands of years and remains a vital crop in drier regions where maize does not grow as well. The ugali made from it is denser and more sustaining.
equipment: Wooden ugali stick or heavy spoon
steps: Bring 3 cups water to a boil.
Mix sorghum flour with remaining 1 cup cold water to a smooth slurry.
Pour slurry into boiling water while stirring constantly.
Stir vigorously over medium-low heat for 12—15 minutes until thick and firm.
Add more flour if needed to achieve the right consistency.
Shape into a mound. Serve hot.
chefTips: Sorghum ugali tends to be slightly stickier than maize ugali — a lightly oiled spoon helps with shaping.
Sorghum takes slightly longer than maize to fully cook through — allow the full 12—15 minutes.
commonMistakes: Not cooking long enough — the ugali will taste raw and starchy.
Too thin — should be firm enough to hold its shape.

faqs.q: What does sorghum ugali taste like?
faqs.a: Slightly earthy and subtly smoky — distinctly different from plain white maize ugali. Those who grew up with it often prefer its more complex flavour.

cookingScience: Sorghum contains more tannins than maize, which contribute to its distinctive slightly astringent flavour and reddish colour. These tannins also have antioxidant properties.
sustainabilityTips: Sorghum is more drought-resistant than maize — a responsible crop choice for climate-uncertain growing conditions.
healthBenefits: Rich in antioxidants from sorghum tannins.
Good source of iron and B vitamins.
culturalNote: Sorghum has been a vital crop in Kenya for thousands of years, particularly in drier regions. Sorghum ugali remains a proud staple in communities where it has been grown and eaten for generations.
